newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish crown seen shaking off EMU blues quickly.
newsitem.headline: Swedish crown seen shaking off EMU blues quickly.

text.p: The Swedish crown will suffer a temporary and limited setback if a radio report proves to be true and the government postpones a link to Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) until 2003, analysts said on Wednesday.

"If membership was to be delayed until 2003 some would probably take a negative view on the crown as people have expected Sweden to join in 2001 or 2002," James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber, told Reuters.
"But the weakening is likely to be temporary and fairly limited," he said.
McKay expected the currency to soften to 4.57 crowns to the mark for a couple of days after such an announcement and then rebound to the recent level of around 4.50.
Sven-Arne Svensson, chief economist at Hagstromer & Qviberg brokerage, saw the crown softening a few percent in a temporary dip for a couple of weeks.

The crown has softened about seven percent since October on worldwide uncertainty about EMU and worries that the Swedish government has decided to loosen the fiscal austerity measures it introduced in 1994 to regain voter support.

On Wednesday the crown weakened as market players started to worry about Sweden's EMU stance after a radio report. At 1315 GMT the crown was changing hands at 4.5140 against the mark compared to a late Tuesday quote of 4.4920.

Radio news said Prime Minister Goran Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink had agreed the country should not join EMU in the next parliamentary term 1998-2002 unless new general elections were held.

The radio concluded that Swedish EMU membership would be delayed until 2003, after the next parliamentary elections in the autumn of 2002, unless the government took the unusual decision to call a snap election.
"I don't think there will be an extra election," Svensson said, dismissing the radio report as speculation.
Opinion polls show Swedes are fairly hostile to further European integration.

The most recent poll, published on May 6, showed 35 percent of Swedes were against EMU, while 26 percent wanted the country to join EMU from its start in 1999, 24 percent wanted to wait and see and 15 percent were undecided.
In addition, the Social Democrats are split on the issue.

The party's executive party committee will take its decision at a meeting this Friday or next week, Prime Minister Goran Persson said on Tuesday. A decision must be made before a party meeting on June 23.
Analysts said French elections at the weekend were likely to overshadow any announcement Sweden may make on Friday.
"When players wake up on Monday they will have the French election to focus on," McKay said.
With a "No" to EMU pushing the crown to softer levels for a while, dealers will eventually note strong Swedish fundamentals again and the currency will rebound, analysts said.
"People will start looking at fundamentals again - the low inflation and the strong current account," Svensson said.
